title: Watch sunrise light hit Machu Picchu from the Sun Gate
description: Entry tickets sell out months ahead in high season, and only a few hundred Sun Gate arrivals catch the light before the cloud rolls in. Book the first entry slot if you want the postcard shot without the rope-line crowd.

title: Climb Huayna Picchu for the aerial view over Machu Picchu
description: Only 400 permits are issued per day, split into two entry times, and they attach to a specific Machu Picchu ticket booked weeks in advance. The final stretch is a near-vertical scramble on Inca-cut steps with a chain handrail.

title: Trek the classic four-day Inca Trail to Machu Picchu
description: The trail closes every February for maintenance and permits, 500 a day including guides and porters, sell out four to six months ahead in peak season. Dead Woman's Pass at 4,215m is the point most people question their choices.

title: Trace the zigzag stone walls of Sacsayhuaman above Cusco
description: Some of the fitted andesite blocks weigh over 100 tonnes and were cut with no mortar, gaps too tight for a blade. It's a 20-minute uphill walk from the Plaza de Armas, useful for acclimatising before the Inca Trail.

title: Watch evening light hit the cathedral from Cusco's Plaza de Armas
description: The cathedral was built directly over the demolished palace of Inca Wiracocha using stones looted from Sacsayhuaman. Inside, a Cusco-school painting reworks the Last Supper with a plate of roast guinea pig as the main course.

title: Climb the terraces of Ollantaytambo, a still-living Inca town
description: Unlike most Inca sites, Ollantaytambo's original street grid and water channels are still in daily use by the families living in them. The unfinished Temple of the Sun shows exactly how the enormous stone blocks were dragged and stacked.

title: Walk the Pisac ruins terraces and browse the Sunday market
description: The ruins above town see a fraction of Machu Picchu's crowds despite equally dramatic terracing and an intact Inca cemetery pocked with looted tombs. The market is best on Sunday, when villages from the surrounding valley bring produce and textiles down.

title: See Moray's farming terraces and the salt pans of Maras
description: Moray's terraced bowl creates a 15C temperature gradient between top and bottom, thought to be an Inca crop laboratory. Ten minutes away, over 3,000 salt pools fed by a subterranean spring have been worked by the same families since Inca times.

title: Hike to Rainbow Mountain before the afternoon cloud rolls in
description: The mineral stripes were only exposed by melting snow around 2015, and the trailhead sits at 4,600m before an already steep climb - altitude, not distance, is what wrecks people. Start at 3am with the first tour buses if you want the ridge to yourself.

title: Hike up to the turquoise water of Laguna Humantay
description: The glacial lake sits at 4,200m and its colour comes from suspended rock flour, brightest around midday sun. It's now a common detour on the Salkantay trek, but also works as a standalone day trip from Cusco.

title: Trek two days in to reach Choquequirao before the crowds do
description: Larger than Machu Picchu but reachable only by a two-day descent-and-climb trek, it gets a few dozen visitors a day instead of thousands. A cable car has been proposed for years but hasn't been built, so the walk is still the only way in.

title: Step onto a hand-built reed island on Lake Titicaca
description: The islands are woven from totora reed and re-layered every few weeks as the base rots from below, so walking on one feels like walking on a mattress. Go early, before the tour boats from Puno arrive in convoy.

title: Watch Taquile islanders knit their own social status into their hats
description: Men on Taquile knit, not weave, a skill passed down as a rite of passage, and the caps they wear signal marital status at a glance. There are no cars or hotels on the island, just a steep staircase up from the dock.

title: Spend the night with a host family on Amantani Island
description: Homestays are rotated between families by the community so tourism income is shared evenly. The climb to the twin hilltop temples of Pachatata and Pachamama for sunset over the lake is the reason to stay rather than day-trip.

title: See the Colla funeral towers of Sillustani at sunset
description: The tallest chullpa burial towers stand 12m high, built with a stonework precision the Inca later adopted, some predating Cusco's empire. Grave robbers left most of them cracked open, but the site on a peninsula over Lake Umayo is close to empty most afternoons.

title: Watch condors ride the thermals at Cruz del Condor
description: Andean condors use the canyon's morning thermals to launch, so arrive by 8am - by 10am most have soared off to feed. Colca is nearly twice the depth of the Grand Canyon, though the viewpoint doesn't advertise that.

title: Get lost in the painted streets of Santa Catalina Monastery
description: A walled citadel-within-a-city that housed cloistered nuns for over 400 years and wasn't opened to the public until 1970. The ochre, blue and terracotta streets inside are named after Spanish cities and were only ever meant to be seen by the sisters who lived there.

title: Summit the perfect cone of El Misti volcano overnight
description: The two-day climb tops out at 5,822m, and most operators push for the summit at 2am to catch sunrise and descend before the afternoon wind picks up. Acclimatise in Arequipa (2,335m) for at least two days first or the altitude will end the trip for you.

title: Trek down into Colca Canyon to the Sangalle oasis
description: The descent from Cabanaconde to the palm-fringed 'Oasis' at the canyon floor drops over 1,000m on a dusty switchback trail, and the climb back out the next morning is the part nobody mentions in advance. Bring more water than feels necessary.

title: Fly over the Nazca Lines to see the hummingbird and the monkey
description: The geoglyphs are only legible from the air, and the small planes bank hard and repeatedly so both sides get a view - motion sickness tablets are worth taking beforehand. Morning flights avoid the thermal turbulence that grounds afternoon slots.

title: Climb the roadside mirador for a free look at the Nazca Lines
description: The metal tower beside the Pan-American Highway shows only two figures, the hands and the tree, at an angle, nothing like the flight - but it costs a few soles instead of over a hundred dollars. A reasonable stop if a flight isn't in the budget.

title: Sandboard the dunes around the Huacachina oasis at golden hour
description: Dune buggies haul you to the top of dunes over 100m high for a stomach-drop descent before the sunset run, which is the timing worth booking for. The oasis lagoon itself has shrunk over the decades and is now partly topped up artificially.

title: Cruise past sea lions and penguins at the Ballestas Islands
description: Nicknamed the 'poor man's Galapagos', the boat doesn't land but gets close enough for Humboldt penguins, sea lion colonies and the occasional condor overhead. Boats leave early to beat the wind that picks up by mid-morning.

title: Taste pisco straight from the still at an Ica bodega
description: Ica is Peru's pisco heartland, and small family bodegas still press grapes the traditional way in stone troughs. Harvest and distillation run March to May, so that window is when the bodegas are actually working rather than just pouring for tours.

The reddish sand comes from eroded granite cliffs mixing with black volcanic rock, and it's a detour most Ballestas Islands day-trippers skip entirely. There's no shade and no facilities, so treat it as a lookout stop rather than a swim.
title: Find the ochre sand of Playa Roja in Paracas National Reserve
Descend into the bone-lined catacombs under San Francisco Church
description: An estimated 25,000 people are buried in the tunnels beneath the monastery, and some chambers arrange femurs and skulls into geometric patterns rather than piles. It was Lima's main cemetery until the early 1800s and stayed sealed and forgotten until 1943.

title: Eat ceviche for lunch in Miraflores, the way locals actually do
description: Ceviche is a lunch dish in Peru, not a dinner one - the fish is cut to order and most serious cevicherias close by 5pm. The leftover citrus-chilli marinade, leche de tigre, is often served as a shot before the plate arrives.

title: Cross the Bridge of Sighs in Barranco holding your breath
description: Local legend says if you cross while holding your breath your wish comes true - a short enough bridge that most people manage it. The surrounding streets carry some of Lima's best street art and turn into an open-air party most weekend nights.

title: Tour the adobe pyramid of Huaca Pucllana lit up after dark
description: A pre-Inca Lima-culture pyramid built from adobe bricks stacked on edge, like a bookshelf rather than flat, to survive earthquakes, standing in the middle of a modern Miraflores neighbourhood. The night tour lights the ramps and excavated tombs differently to the daytime visit.

title: Walk the pyramid complex of Pachacamac outside Lima
description: A pilgrimage site and oracle temple that predates the Inca by centuries and was still functioning when the Spanish arrived, who later built a convent on top of it. It's 40 minutes from Miraflores and gets a fraction of the visitors of sites in Cusco.

title: Walk the adobe walls of Chan Chan, the world's largest mud-brick city
description: The Chimu capital once housed an estimated 30,000 people across ten walled royal compounds, its walls carved with friezes of fish and pelicans repeated across entire courtyards. El Nino rains have eroded whole sections over the last century, so the restored Tschudi complex is the part still worth the entry fee.

title: Watch fishermen paddle centuries-old caballito reed boats at Huanchaco
description: Local fishermen still ride the same reed-boat design depicted on 3,000-year-old Moche pottery, straddling them like a horse (caballito) to paddle out past the break. The town also has a legitimate, mellow point break beginners can handle.

title: Spend a night in an Amazon jungle lodge reachable only by boat from Iquitos
description: Iquitos is the largest city in the world unreachable by road - everyone arrives by plane or boat. Lodges an hour or more downriver run night caiman-spotting trips and canopy walkways that day-trippers from the city dock never reach.

title: Spot pink river dolphins in the Pacaya-Samiria reserve
description: Peru's largest protected wetland is nicknamed the 'mirror of the jungle' for its flooded-forest reflections, and boat access changes completely between high water (roughly December to May) and low water months. A multi-day river trip is the only way in - there's no road or day-trip version.

title: Walk the floating stilt-house market of Belen
description: Known locally as the 'Venice of the Amazon', the neighbourhood floats or stands on stilts depending on the river level, and the market sells jungle produce found nowhere else, including bark, grubs and fruit with no English name. Go with a guide; it's a real neighbourhood, not a tourist set.

title: Hike to the glacial-blue water of Laguna 69
description: The trailhead alone sits at 3,850m and the lake at 4,600m, so the altitude gain hurts more than the 9km distance suggests. It's the single most-hiked trail out of Huaraz for a reason - meltwater off Nevado Chacraraju turns the lake an almost unreal blue.

title: Explore the underground galleries of Chavin de Huantar
description: This temple complex predates the Inca by over 2,000 years, and its stone tenon heads and underground acoustic passages were built to disorient pilgrims during hallucinogenic rituals. A network of stone ducts still channels water through the galleries the way it did 3,000 years ago.

title: Ride the cable car up to the fortress of Kuelap
description: Called the 'Machu Picchu of the north', this Chachapoya cloud-fortress predates the Inca and once held around 400 circular stone houses inside walls up to 19m tall. A cable car opened in 2017 cut what used to be a multi-hour climb down to 20 minutes.

title: Hike through cloud forest to the base of Gocta waterfall
description: At around 770m it's one of the tallest waterfalls in the world, yet it wasn't formally measured and mapped for outsiders until 2005 - locals had kept it quiet, believing a mermaid and a serpent guarded it. The hike in is humid and muddy regardless of season; proper boots matter more than timing.

title: Learn to surf the point break at Mancora
description: Mancora's wave is forgiving enough for first-timers, which is why the town doubles as Peru's party-beach destination, loudest December through February. For the serious break, surfers head an hour south to Cabo Blanco or Puerto Chicama instead.

title: See the untouched royal tomb of the Lord of Sipan
description: Discovered in 1987, this Moche tomb was the richest unlooted burial ever found in the Americas, and the museum reconstructs the burial chamber exactly as archaeologists found it, gold mask and all. It gets a fraction of Cusco's visitor numbers despite the find being compared to Tutankhamun's tomb.

title: Watch dozens of macaws feed at a Tambopata clay lick at dawn
description: Macaws and parrots gather at exposed riverbank clay to neutralise toxins in the seeds they eat, and dawn is the only reliable window before they scatter for the day. Reaching the reserve means a flight to Puerto Maldonado followed by hours upriver by boat.

title: Ride the cog train up to Christ the Redeemer on Corcovado
description: The 38m Art Deco statue took nine years to build and stands on a peak inside Tijuca National Park, the largest urban rainforest in the world. Clear-sky slots fill first online - go early morning before the cloud that regularly swallows the summit by midday.

title: Take the two-stage cable car up Sugarloaf Mountain for sunset
description: The original 1912 cable car system still runs, now updated to glass-sided cars that swap between two peaks. Sunset is the busiest slot for a reason: the whole bay, Christ the Redeemer and Copacabana line up in one 360-degree view.

title: Walk the wave-pattern promenade along Copacabana Beach at dawn
description: The black-and-white Portuguese stone mosaic underfoot was laid in 1970 and copies a Lisbon pavement pattern. Locals do their exercise laps before 7am, before the beach fills and the afternoon sun gets fierce.

title: Watch the sunset crowd applaud from Ipanema's Arpoador rocks
description: Arpoador, the rocky point between Ipanema and Copacabana, is the one spot in Rio where the sun sets directly into the ocean, and regulars genuinely clap when it drops below the horizon. The beach itself is informally zoned by numbered lifeguard posts, each with its own crowd.

title: Climb the mosaic-tiled Selaron Steps in Lapa
description: Chilean artist Jorge Selaron covered these 215 steps in tiles from over 60 countries, sent to him by visitors after his work gained a following, and kept adding to it until his death in 2013. It sits a block from Lapa's arches, best combined with an evening out in the neighbourhood's samba bars.

title: Hike through Tijuca National Park to the Pedra Bonita viewpoint
description: The forest covering Rio's hills is entirely replanted - it was cleared for coffee plantations in the 1800s and replanted by hand starting in 1861 to protect the city's water supply. Pedra Bonita is also the hang-gliding launch point, so expect company circling overhead.

title: Tour the Maracana, Brazil's cathedral of football
description: Built for the 1950 World Cup final, it once held an official crowd of nearly 200,000 - modern safety rules cap it at a still-enormous 78,000. Match-day tickets are far cheaper and easier to get than European football, so catch a Flamengo game if the calendar lines up.

title: Watch samba schools parade the Sambodromo at Carnival
description: Each samba school gets exactly 65 to 75 minutes to parade with up to 3,000 dancers and a purpose-built float, and judges dock points for going over. Grandstand tickets for the top two nights sell out by December; the practical alternative is watching a rehearsal parade earlier in the season.

title: Wander the car-free cobblestones of colonial Paraty
description: Portuguese gold-route traders built Paraty's streets to flood deliberately at high tide, flushing the sewage into the bay - they still do. The historic centre bans cars entirely, and cachaca distilleries around town offer tastings of the spirit Paraty has made since the 1600s.

No cars are allowed on the island, so every beach, including Lopes Mendes, regularly ranked among Brazil's best, is reached on foot or by boat. It's two hours from Rio by bus and ferry, yet gets a fraction of Ilhabela or Buzios' crowds.
title: Hike between hidden beaches on car-free Ilha Grande
Cycle Ibirapuera Park past Sao Paulo's modernist museums
description: Oscar Niemeyer designed the park's curved concrete marquee, the Marquise, and several of the museum buildings inside it. Sunday mornings close it to cars entirely for cyclists and rollerbladers, the liveliest time to visit.

title: Eat a mortadella sandwich the size of your head at Mercado Municipal
description: The market's Bar do Mane mortadella sandwich, stacked with a quarter-kilo of meat, has been the signature order for decades and draws a queue by 11am. The stained-glass windows upstairs depicting rural harvest scenes are worth the neck ache.

title: Sail between waterfalls and beaches around Ilhabela
description: Ilhabela is almost entirely covered by Atlantic Forest reserve, with over 30 waterfalls tumbling down to its beaches, several reachable only by boat. It's also Brazil's sailing capital, hosting national regattas most of the summer.

title: Walk the colonial cobblestones of Salvador's Pelourinho
description: The pastel-coloured colonial core takes its name from the whipping post that once stood in its main square, a brutal reminder that Salvador was the largest slave port in the Americas. That same history built Bahia's Afro-Brazilian culture, which is now what the neighbourhood is loudest about celebrating.

title: Watch a capoeira roda play out in a Pelourinho square
description: Developed by enslaved Africans and disguised as dance to evade a ban on martial arts, capoeira is still practised in informal street circles most evenings around Pelourinho. Drop a few reais in the hat if you stop to watch - most circles are semi-professional and this is their income.

title: Trek to the blue grotto pools of Chapada Diamantina
description: The park's Poco Encantado cave has a beam of midday sunlight hitting crystal-clear water so precisely that it only lights up the full 60m depth for part of the year. Cachoeira da Fumaca, one of Brazil's tallest waterfalls, disperses into mist before it hits the ground.

title: Island-hop by boat to the car-free village of Morro de Sao Paulo
description: No cars or paved roads reach the village - everything moves by wheelbarrow cart from the pier. Its five numbered beaches get progressively quieter the further you walk from the lighthouse, with the fourth and fifth practically empty on weekdays.

title: Visit rescued sea turtles at the Praia do Forte conservation project
description: Projeto Tamar started here in 1982 and is credited with pulling several Brazilian sea turtle species back from the edge of extinction; the on-site pools let you see species you won't spot snorkelling. Nesting season runs September to March if you want a chance at hatchlings.

title: Base yourself in the hillside village of Vale do Capao
description: A dirt-road village of artisans and trekking guides at the edge of Chapada Diamantina, popular with Brazilians long before international tourists found the park's waterfalls. It's the quieter, cheaper base camp compared to Lencois, the town most tours default to.

title: Get soaked at the Devil's Throat walkway on the Brazilian side
description: Brazil's side of the falls has only about 20% of the total drop but the best panoramic view, a single trail ending on a walkway that puts you directly above the Devil's Throat's spray. Bring a dry bag - the mist here is heavier than a light rain.

title: Walk through free-flying toucan aviaries at Parque das Aves
description: Unlike most bird parks, several enclosures here are walk-through, so toucans, macaws and hummingbirds fly at head height around visitors. It sits right across from the falls entrance, easy to pair with the same morning.

title: Tour the turbine hall of the Itaipu hydroelectric dam
description: For decades Itaipu was the largest hydroelectric plant on earth and still supplies close to 90% of Paraguay's electricity from a dam shared between the two countries. The special technical tour goes inside the turbine floor, well beyond what the standard panoramic visit shows.

title: Boat the rivers of Porto Jofre for the best jaguar odds in the Pantanal
description: This stretch of the Cuiaba and Piquiri rivers has one of the highest densities of wild jaguars on the planet, with sightings odds during dry season running well above 90% for a multi-day stay. Boats are the only way in - there's no road once the Transpantaneira ends.

title: Drive the wildlife-lined dirt of the Transpantaneira Highway
description: A raised dirt road built over more than 120 wooden bridges, many left unrepaired for years, so punctures and washouts are part of the trip. Caimans sun themselves on the verges in such numbers that after the first hour you stop stopping the car for them.

title: Snorkel the transparent rivers of Bonito
description: Limestone filters the rivers here to near-swimming-pool clarity, and the Rio da Prata float lets you drift face-down over fish for over a kilometre without swimming a stroke. Access to every river is by permit through a licensed operator; there's no independent version of this.

title: Descend into the electric-blue cave lake of Gruta do Lago Azul
description: The underground lake's blue is most intense between roughly November and February, when sunlight hits the water at the right angle through the cave mouth. Access is capped by timed groups to protect the formations, so book the slot rather than showing up.

title: Swim in a rain-fed lagoon among the white dunes of Lencois Maranhenses
description: The 'sheets' are pure white sand dunes with no vegetation, and the turquoise lagoons only fill between roughly June and September - visit in November and the same view is just dry sand. Locals will tell you which lagoon is deepest that week; it changes.

title: Reach the remote Lagoa Bonita by 4x4 deep inside the dune field
description: Getting past the easy-access lagoons near Barreirinhas to Lagoa Bonita means a rough multi-hour 4x4 crossing or a multi-day trekking traverse from Atins. The reward is a lagoon most day-trippers never reach, without the crowds of the postcard viewpoint.

title: Watch the Rio Negro and Amazon run side by side, unmixed, at the Meeting of the Waters
description: The black, acidic Rio Negro and the pale, sediment-heavy Solimoes run side by side for several kilometres without blending, a difference in temperature, speed and density that's visible as a sharp line straight off the boat. Boats idle right on the seam so you can put one hand in each colour.

title: See an opera inside the jungle-bound Teatro Amazonas
description: Rubber barons shipped Italian marble, French ironwork and Murano glass upriver to build this opera house in 1896, at a time when Manaus had no road link to the rest of Brazil. It still hosts a real season, not just a tourist facade - check the calendar before assuming it's a daytime-only visit.

title: Spend a night in a jungle lodge upriver from Manaus
description: Lodges here run night caiman-spotting trips and canopy tower sunrises, and high-water season (roughly May to July) lets boats push directly into the flooded forest between tree trunks. Low water months instead open up beach camping on exposed river sandbars.

title: Join Manaus locals on the river beach at Ponta Negra in dry season
description: The Rio Negro drops enough between roughly August and November to expose a genuine sand beach right in the city, packed with locals rather than tourists. In high water months the same spot disappears entirely underwater.

title: Snorkel Baia dos Porcos on Fernando de Noronha
description: A daily environmental fee plus a visitor cap keep the island's waters some of the clearest in Brazil, with sea turtles visible from the shoreline most days. August to December brings the calmest, clearest water for snorkelling before the swell picks up.

title: Climb down the cliff staircase to Praia do Sancho
description: Repeatedly voted Brazil's best beach, it's reached by a steep staircase through a crack in the cliff face, not a road. Numbers are capped daily by the park, so arriving right at opening avoids the wait to descend.

title: Watch the sunset from Recife's Marco Zero square
description: Built on reclaimed land at the mouth of the Capibaribe river, the square marks the point the Portuguese first landed in 1535. The Instituto Ricardo Brennand nearby holds one of the largest collections of medieval armour and Dutch colonial art outside Europe, an odd but genuine detour.

title: Wander Olinda's hillside cobblestones during frevo carnival
description: Olinda's carnival runs on frevo, a frenetic brass-band style that requires no couple or samba steps, and giant papier-mache figures parade through streets too narrow and steep for floats. Outside carnival, the same hillside gives the best photo of Recife's skyline across the bay.

title: Climb Ouro Preto's baroque church steps built on gold-rush wealth
description: The town funded some of Brazil's finest baroque architecture, much of it carved by the sculptor Aleijadinho, on wealth from a gold rush so intense an estimated sixth of the world's gold passed through here in the 1700s. The steep streets are cobbled in the original stone; heels are a mistake.

title: Walk contemporary art pavilions set inside a botanical garden at Inhotim
description: Each major artwork gets its own purpose-built pavilion scattered through 140 hectares of landscaped gardens, so seeing it properly means a full day of walking or a golf-cart shuttle. It's one of the largest open-air contemporary art centres in the world, and most international visitors have never heard of it.

title: Tour Niemeyer's modernist Cathedral and Congress in Brasilia
description: The entire city was built from scratch in under four years and opened in 1960, laid out in the shape of an airplane or a bow depending who you ask at the viewing platform. The Cathedral's crown of concrete columns looks crushed by weight until you're standing directly underneath, where it suddenly opens into light.

title: Watch sunset from the dune at Jericoacoara
description: Locals gather on Duna do Por do Sol every clear evening and applaud when the sun drops, a ritual as reliable as the one on Ipanema's rocks. Jericoacoara only got paved road access in 2015; before that the whole town existed at the end of a sand track.

title: Ride a buggy over the red-and-white cliffs of Canoa Quebrada
description: The cliffs here are streaked red, white and ochre from mineral bands, and buggy drivers use them as a launch point for the labirinto dune trails further along the coast. Kitesurfers take over the same stretch of coastline once the trade winds pick up around August.

title: Surf the sandboard dunes and swell of Joaquina Beach
description: Joaquina hosts Brazil's national surf championship most years, and the dunes right behind the beach double as a sandboarding spot on flat days. The island of Florianopolis has over 40 beaches, each with a different personality, from this surf break to family-calm coves on the other coast.

title: Paddleboard the lagoon at Lagoa da Conceicao at sunset
description: The lagoon splits Florianopolis island in two and turns into the social centre of town after dark, ringed by bars that spill onto the sand. Stand-up paddleboard rental stands line the shore and stay open well past sunset in high summer.

title: Watch a tango unfold at a San Telmo milonga
description: San Telmo is where tango is generally agreed to have started, in the brothels and docks of the late 1800s, and the neighbourhood still runs open milongas where anyone can dance, not just paid performers. Sunday's antiques street fair on Defensa is the daytime version of the same neighbourhood energy.

title: Get lost among the marble mausoleums of Recoleta Cemetery
description: Laid out like a miniature city of streets and avenues, it holds over 6,400 elaborate tombs including Eva Peron's, tucked in a modest family vault rather than the grand monument most visitors expect. A resident cat colony has lived among the graves for decades and has its own informal caretakers.

title: Stand where Argentina's history keeps happening, Plaza de Mayo
description: The Madres de Plaza de Mayo still circle the square every Thursday afternoon, a protest tradition started in 1977 demanding answers about children disappeared under the military dictatorship. The pink Casa Rosada behind them gets its colour, by one account, from a 19th-century mix of whitewash and bull's blood.

title: Photograph the corrugated-tin colour of Caminito in La Boca
description: Dock workers originally painted their houses in leftover ship paint, whatever colour was on hand, which is how the clashing rainbow look started. Stick to the pedestrian street itself and the few blocks around La Bombonera stadium; the surrounding barrio has a rougher reputation after dark.

title: Order a full parrillada at a Buenos Aires steakhouse
description: Argentina eats more beef per capita than almost anywhere on earth, and a parrillada mixta brings a share plate of cuts most visitors have never tried, chinchulines and morcilla included. Order it medium-rare (a punto) or the kitchen will assume you want it well done, the local default.

title: Tour the gold-leaf interior of Teatro Colon opera house
description: Acoustically it's ranked among the five best opera houses on earth, a reputation built on marble shipped from Europe and decades of construction that ran from 1889 to 1908. Same-day cheap standing tickets (tertulia) are sold for evening performances if the guided day tour isn't enough.

title: Browse shelves stacked on a converted theatre's stage at El Ateneo
description: The building opened as a 1919 theatre and cinema before being converted into a bookstore in 2000, keeping its frescoed ceiling, opera boxes and red stage curtain intact. The old stage is now a cafe, worth the coffee just to sit under the dome.

Out past the western edge of the city where the old cattle yards used to be, this weekend fair pulls in folk dancers, gaucho horsemanship displays and regional food stalls almost entirely for a local crowd. It's a 40-minute bus or taxi from downtown and worlds away from anything San Telmo sells tourists.
title: Watch gauchos race horses at the Feria de Mataderos folk fair
Watch chunks calve off Perito Moreno Glacier from the boardwalks
description: It's one of the few glaciers on earth still advancing rather than retreating, and the ice face regularly cracks and drops slabs the size of buildings into the lake with a boom you feel before you hear it. The metal walkway system gives multiple viewing levels without a hike required.

title: Strap on crampons and walk the blue ice of Perito Moreno
description: A short boat crossing gets you onto the glacier itself for a guided walk between crevasses, finishing most tours with a whisky poured over glacier ice. Bigger 'ice trekking' routes go further onto the surface than the standard 'mini trekking' option, at extra cost and fitness required.

title: Hike to Laguna de los Tres beneath Mount Fitz Roy
description: The final kilometre is a steep, exposed scramble that regularly turns hikers back in high wind, but it opens onto the postcard view of Fitz Roy's granite spires reflected in a turquoise glacial lake. The trailhead starts directly from El Chalten, no transport needed and no entry fee, unusual for a park this famous.

title: Trek to the Cerro Torre lookout over Laguna Torre
description: Cerro Torre's near-vertical granite spire, often capped by a mushroom of rime ice, was one of the last major peaks in the world to be climbed, and disputed claims over the first ascent ran for decades. The trail is gentler than the Fitz Roy hike, making it the better call on a low-visibility day.

title: Base yourself in Argentina's trekking capital, El Chalten
description: Founded only in 1985, largely to help Argentina's territorial claim against Chile in the area, the town exists almost entirely to service trekkers heading into Los Glaciares National Park. Every trail starts free and unguided right from town, a rarity worth building a multi-day stay around.

title: Get your passport stamped at the end of the world in Ushuaia
description: Ushuaia markets itself hard as 'Fin del Mundo', and the tourist office sells a novelty passport stamp to prove you made it. It's also the main departure point for Antarctica cruises, so the harbour often has a genuine icebreaker or expedition ship docked alongside the fishing boats.

title: Ride the End of the World Train into Tierra del Fuego National Park
description: The narrow-gauge steam train was built in 1902 to haul timber cut by convict labour from the nearby prison, and it now runs a short scenic stretch purely for tourists. Get off partway and hike the rest of the park's coastal trail instead of riding the full loop back.

title: Cruise the Beagle Channel past sea lions and the Lighthouse at the End of the World
description: Named after Darwin's ship, the channel splits Argentina and Chile and its small rocky islands are packed with sea lion colonies and cormorant nests. Full-day versions add a landing on Bridges Island for a short walk and hot chocolate rather than just a photo pass of the lighthouse.

title: Hike up to Martial Glacier for the view back down over Ushuaia
description: A chairlift cuts out the first stretch of the climb, leaving a rougher scramble up scree to the glacier face itself. In winter the same slope becomes Ushuaia's small in-town ski area, unusual for a glacier hike anywhere else in the world.

title: Walk the catwalk over the Devil's Throat on the Argentine side
description: A long metal walkway crosses the Iguazu River directly above the point where 14 separate falls converge, putting you at the rim looking straight down rather than across at it like the Brazilian viewpoint. The park's little train saves the twenty-minute walk to the trailhead if you're short on time.

title: Take the boat under the base of the falls on the Gran Aventura
description: The boat drives directly into the spray at the base of the San Martin falls, close enough that ponchos are handed out but everyone gets soaked regardless. It's a separate ticket and trail system, the Lower and Upper Circuits, from the Devil's Throat walkway, so budget a full day to do both properly.

title: Walk the red sandstone ruins of the San Ignacio Mini Jesuit mission
description: Founded in 1610, this was one of over 30 Jesuit reductions built to convert and protect Guarani communities before the order was expelled in 1767 and the jungle reclaimed most of them. An evening light-and-sound show projected onto the ruins runs most nights, telling the mission's history across the stonework itself.

title: Cycle between Malbec wineries in Mendoza's Lujan de Cuyo
description: Mendoza's high-altitude desert vineyards, most over 900m, are what give Argentine Malbec its intensity, and Lujan de Cuyo and the Uco Valley are dense enough with bodegas to cycle between tastings. Harvest season, roughly late February to April, adds grape-stomping festivals on top of the usual tastings.

title: Look up at Aconcagua, the tallest peak outside the Himalayas
description: At 6,961m it's the highest mountain in both the western and southern hemispheres, and the Confluencia viewpoint trail gets you a proper look at it without needing the multi-week expedition permit serious climbers require. Around 3,000 people attempt the summit each season; roughly a third make it.

title: Rent a bike and wobble between Maipu's family wineries
description: Maipu is close enough to Mendoza city for a bike-and-wine day trip without a driver, with small family bodegas, an olive oil mill and an absinthe distillery all within pedalling distance of each other. Pace the tastings; several visitors a year genuinely do fall off on the ride back.

title: See the sulphur-stained natural bridge at Puente del Inca
description: The bridge formed naturally over thermal sulphur springs that stain the rock a deep mustard yellow, and the ruins of an old spa hotel destroyed by an avalanche still sit half-buried beneath it. It's a roadside stop on the route toward the Chilean border, easily combined with an Aconcagua viewpoint trip.

title: See the seven-coloured hillside above Purmamarca
description: The mineral bands, from iron oxide reds to manganese purples, formed over 65 million years and are most vivid in the low light just after sunrise. A short walking circuit behind the village, the Paseo de los Colorados, gets you closer than the roadside viewpoint everyone else stops at.

title: Walk the blinding white crust of the Salinas Grandes salt flat
description: At over 3,400m, this is a smaller, easier day trip than Bolivia's Uyuni but the same forced-perspective photos work here, salt crust cracked into geometric tiles for kilometres in every direction. Bring sunglasses; the glare off the white salt is fierce even on a cloudy day.

title: Wander the colonial streets of Humahuaca at 2,940m
description: The town anchors the northern end of the Quebrada de Humahuaca, a UNESCO-listed valley that was a trade route for over 10,000 years before the Inca or the Spanish arrived. Altitude hits harder here than in Purmamarca; ease into the day rather than climbing straight to the hilltop monument.

title: Ride the Train to the Clouds across a viaduct at 4,200m
description: The line was built in the 1920s to move freight across the Andes and climbs through 21 tunnels and two zigzags to cross the La Polvorilla viaduct, 63m above the valley floor. Altitude sickness is common enough on board that the train carries oxygen; the ride is scenic but not a light undertaking.

title: Ride the cable car up Cerro San Bernardo for the view over Salta
description: The cable car climbs 1,300m above the city in under ten minutes, or you can walk up the roughly 1,000 steps if the altitude and heat don't put you off. Salta's colonial plaza and cathedral, one of the best-preserved in Argentina, are laid out directly below.

title: Taste high-altitude Torrontes at a Cafayate bodega
description: Cafayate's vineyards sit above 1,700m, among the highest wine country on earth, which is what gives the local Torrontes grape its sharp, floral character found almost nowhere else. The drive down from Salta through the Quebrada de las Conchas passes red rock formations worth the stops alone.

title: Watch southern right whales breach off Peninsula Valdes
description: Southern right whales come this close to shore to breed and calve that sightings from the beach at Puerto Piramides are common, no boat required, though the boat tours get genuinely alongside them. The peninsula's cliffs also hold elephant seal colonies and one of the few spots where orcas intentionally beach themselves to hunt sea lion pups, a rare behaviour filmed here for decades.

title: Walk among a million Magellanic penguins at Punta Tombo
description: It's the largest Magellanic penguin colony outside Antarctica, and marked trails let you walk within a few metres of nesting burrows without disturbing them. Numbers peak in November and December when chicks hatch; by April the entire colony has swum north for winter.

title: Take Welsh tea at a Gaiman tea house
description: Welsh settlers founded Gaiman in 1874 and the town still runs tea houses serving a full Welsh spread of scones, cakes and black tea, a tradition that survived even as the Welsh language nearly disappeared from daily use. Princess Diana's 1995 visit to one tea house is still the thing every waiter mentions.

title: Drive the Circuito Chico past Bariloche's lakes and chocolate shops
description: Swiss and German settlers brought chocolate-making traditions here a century ago, and the town now has one of the highest concentrations of chocolate shops anywhere in South America, most doing free tastings. The Circuito Chico driving loop strings together lake viewpoints without needing more than a rental car and an afternoon.

title: Ski South America's largest resort at Cerro Catedral
description: With over 1,200 hectares of skiable terrain, it's the biggest ski area in South America and draws Northern Hemisphere racers training through their own off-season. Even non-skiers ride the gondola up for the panorama over Nahuel Huapi Lake.

title: Spot capybara and caiman by boat in the Ibera Wetlands
description: Argentina's second-largest wetland after the Pantanal holds around 30% of the country's biodiversity, and reintroduction programs have brought giant anteaters and jaguars back after decades of local extinction. Access is by small lodge rather than mass tourism infrastructure, so book ahead rather than expecting to show up.

title: Drive the lunar rock formations of Ischigualasto by caravan
description: Nicknamed Valle de la Luna for its eroded rock formations, the park holds some of the most complete dinosaur fossil records from the Triassic period anywhere on earth. Visits are strictly by guided vehicle caravan on a fixed one-way loop; independent driving isn't allowed.

title: Walk beneath Talampaya's 150m red sandstone canyon walls
description: The canyon shares the same Triassic geology and fossil record as neighbouring Ischigualasto, and its sheer walls create an echo chamber so precise that guides demonstrate it with a recording of an ancient dinosaur call. Wind erosion has carved isolated towers locals nicknamed 'the cathedral' and 'the monk' further down the canyon.

title: Tour the Jesuit Block that once ran Cordoba's colonial university
description: Built from the early 1600s, the Manzana Jesuitica housed South America's third-oldest university alongside a church and residence, all still standing and now UNESCO-listed. The Jesuits ran it as the intellectual centre of colonial Cordoba until their expulsion from Spanish America in 1767.

title: Wander the graffiti-covered hills of Valparaiso by funicular
description: Valparaiso's surviving funiculars, built by British-linked rail companies in the early 1900s, are the practical way up its impossibly steep hills, and most are still in daily local use rather than tourist novelties. The Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepcion neighbourhoods carry the densest concentration of street art, much of it legal and revolving as new work covers old.

title: Relax on Vina del Mar's beaches after Valparaiso's hills
description: Chileans call it the 'Garden City' for its manicured parks and flower clock, a deliberate contrast to Valparaiso's gritty, hillside chaos next door. The Pacific here runs cold year-round thanks to the Humboldt Current, so swimming is more a summer dip than a tropical soak.

title: Taste cool-climate Sauvignon Blanc in the Casablanca Valley
description: Ocean fog rolling in most mornings keeps this valley cooler than Chile's other wine regions, which is why it's become the country's benchmark for Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay rather than the reds Chile is better known for. It sits directly between Santiago and Valparaiso, an easy stop on the way to the coast.

title: Visit Pablo Neruda's ship-shaped house at Isla Negra
description: Neruda designed the house like a ship's cabin, crammed with figureheads, shells and nautical instruments collected over decades, and asked to be buried there facing the ocean. It's the least visited of his three house-museums, and arguably the most personal.

title: Watch sunrise line up behind the 15 moai of Ahu Tongariki
description: It's the largest ahu ever built, and the moai standing on it today are a 1990s reconstruction after a 1960 tsunami scattered them across the coastline. Sunrise here is genuinely worth the early alarm; the statues backlit against the sky is the single most photographed shot on the island.

title: Walk the moai quarry where hundreds of statues were abandoned mid-carve
description: Almost 400 moai in every stage of completion still sit in and around this volcanic crater, including some buried up to their necks in erosion, exactly as work stopped centuries ago. It's the closest thing to an open, unanswered mystery left on the island: nobody fully agrees why production halted so abruptly.

title: Stand at the Orongo birdman ceremonial village on the crater rim
description: Built into a crater rim above a 300m drop to the ocean, Orongo hosted an annual competition where clan representatives swam to a nearby islet and raced back with the first sooty tern egg of the season. The petroglyphs of the birdman figure carved into rock here mark a religious shift away from moai-building in the island's final Polynesian era.

title: Swim at Anakena, the palm-fringed beach where moai still stand
description: Oral history holds this as the beach where the island's founding king first landed, and it's one of only two sand beaches on an otherwise rocky, volcanic coastline. Ahu Nau Nau's moai stand right at the treeline, so it's a rare chance to swim and see restored statues in the same view.

title: Watch sunset turn Valle de la Luna's dunes rust red
description: Wind and ancient salt deposits carved this valley into ridges and dunes so lunar-looking that NASA has tested Mars rover equipment nearby. Sunset is the only time visitors are allowed inside, timed to a strict entry and exit window the park enforces closely.

title: Watch El Tatio's geysers erupt at sunrise, the world's highest geyser field
description: At 4,320m, the geysers perform best right at dawn when the cold air makes the steam columns tower highest before the sun burns them off within an hour. The pre-dawn drive from San Pedro takes about 90 minutes and is genuinely below freezing, whatever the desert did during the day before.

title: Look through a telescope under some of the clearest skies on earth
description: Zero light pollution and over 300 cloudless nights a year are why professional observatories cluster in this desert, and several tour operators run amateur sessions with serious telescopes rather than just naked-eye pointing. The Milky Way's core is visible with startling clarity most nights, something even seasoned stargazers from northern latitudes aren't prepared for.

title: Float in the hyper-salty water of Laguna Cejar
description: The salt concentration here is even higher than the Dead Sea's, so floating takes no effort at all, though the salt stings any small cut you didn't know you had. A freshwater shower on site is non-negotiable afterward; the salt residue dries on skin fast in desert air.

title: Watch three flamingo species feed on the Salar de Atacama
description: Chile's largest salt flat is a working lithium mining site as well as a nature reserve, and its shallow lagoons attract Andean, Chilean and rare James's flamingos feeding side by side. The altiplano light here is intense enough that sunglasses are not optional, even on an overcast day.

Iron oxide staining turns the volcanic rock here a deep rust red against a turquoise altiplano lagoon, at over 4,000m near the Bolivian border, a genuine detour past the standard Atacama circuit most day tours stick to. Locals in San Pedro will tell you it beats Laguna Cejar; getting there just takes a full day rather than an afternoon.
title: Reach the red-rock lagoon of Piedras Rojas near the Bolivian border
Ride the funicular up Cerro San Cristobal for the Andes skyline
description: A funicular built in 1925 climbs to a hilltop Virgin Mary statue and, on a clear day, a full snow-capped Andes backdrop behind the city. Locals treat the park at the base as a genuine weekend gym, not just a tourist stop.

title: Hike the canyon trails of Cajon del Maipo outside Santiago
description: An hour from Santiago's traffic, the canyon opens onto glacial rivers, hot springs and the striking blue-green Embalse El Yeso reservoir. It's the default weekend escape for Santiago locals, so trailhead parking fills up fast on any clear Saturday.

title: Taste Cabernet Sauvignon in the Maipo Valley, Chile's oldest wine region
description: Vines were first planted here in the 1830s, making Maipo the origin point of Chile's modern wine industry, and its gravelly soils are still considered the country's best for Cabernet. Several wineries are close enough to Santiago for a half-day trip without an overnight stay.

title: Hike the W Trek beneath Torres del Paine's granite towers
description: The trek is named for the shape it traces on a map, roughly 70-80km over four to five days between the three towers, the French Valley and Grey Glacier. Refugios and campsites must be booked individually months ahead in peak season; showing up without reservations can mean being turned away at the park gate.

title: Kayak past floating icebergs at Grey Glacier
description: The glacier calves house-sized icebergs into Grey Lake, and guided kayak trips thread between them at a safe distance, close enough to hear the ice groan. It's also reachable by catamaran for a lower-effort version of essentially the same view.

title: See the giant sloth remains that started Patagonia's tourism boom at Cueva del Milodon
description: A German settler found preserved skin and bones of an extinct giant ground sloth in this cave in 1896, a discovery that helped put remote Patagonia on the map for European explorers and scientists. A life-size sloth replica now stands at the cave mouth, more amusing than accurate to what was actually found.

title: Walk among 60,000 penguins on Isla Magdalena
description: A two-hour boat crossing from Punta Arenas through the Strait of Magellan reaches this island reserve, where a fixed rope path lets you walk through the colony without disturbing nesting burrows. Numbers peak during breeding season; by April most of the colony has already headed back out to sea.

title: Photograph the stilt houses of Chiloe's palafitos
description: Built directly over the water on wooden stilts in towns like Castro, palafitos let fishing families dock their boats beneath their own kitchens at high tide. Many now operate as guesthouses and restaurants, so it's possible to actually stay in one rather than just photograph it from a bridge.

title: Step inside a UNESCO-listed wooden church on Chiloe
description: Built entirely without nails using Jesuit shipbuilding techniques from the 1700s, 16 of these wooden churches across the archipelago are collectively UNESCO-listed, each painted a slightly different pastel colour by its own community. The church at Achao is the oldest surviving example, dating to 1730.

title: See two penguin species nesting together at Punihuil
description: This is the only place on earth where Humboldt and Magellanic penguins nest on the same beach, and boats keep a fixed distance rather than landing to protect the colony. Choppy Pacific swell here can cancel or shorten trips with little notice, so build in a spare day if seeing it matters.

title: Hike the glacier slopes of the perfectly conical Osorno Volcano
description: Its symmetrical cone, often compared to Japan's Mount Fuji, rises directly above Lake Llanquihue and last erupted in 1869, calmer these days than its more active neighbour Villarrica. A small ski lift operates in winter, but summer visits mean crampons and a guide for the upper glacier sections.

title: Climb Villarrica to peer into its lava-lit crater
description: It's one of the few volcanoes on earth where you can look directly down into an active, glowing lava lake from the crater rim, weather and activity levels permitting. Rangers close the climb without notice when seismic activity ticks up, so confirm on the morning of, not the day before.

title: Soak in a forest hot spring after a day in Pucon
description: Volcanic activity across the region feeds dozens of natural hot springs in the forest around Pucon, ranging from developed resort pools to rustic riverside soaks reached by dirt road. Most locals rate the less-developed ones higher; ask at your accommodation rather than booking the first one that shows up online.

title: Drive a stretch of the Carretera Austral through Patagonian wilderness
description: Built by the Pinochet government starting in 1976 to connect Chile's most isolated region, over 1,200km of it is still unpaved gravel, ferry-linked in several places where the road simply stops at a fjord. Fuel stations are hours apart in places, so tank up whenever you see one, not when the gauge says to.

title: Kayak into the Marble Caves' swirling blue chambers
description: Thousands of years of wave action on General Carrera Lake's calcium carbonate rock carved these caverns, and the exact colour of the water and walls shifts with the lake's water level through the year. Kayaking gets you inside chambers the standard boat tour only glides past.

title: Hike to the glacier that hangs off a cliff at Queulat
description: The glacier clings to a cliff face high above the valley floor, occasionally shedding waterfalls and ice chunks that free-fall into the lagoon below. It's directly beside the Carretera Austral, one of the easiest hikes to combine with the road trip itself rather than requiring a detour.

title: Taste bold reds in the Colchagua Valley by horse-drawn cart or vintage car
description: Considered Chile's premier red wine region, Colchagua's warm days and cool nights suit the Carmenere grape especially well, a variety once thought extinct in France and rediscovered growing here, misidentified as Merlot, in 1994. Several wineries run vintage-car tours between tastings instead of the usual shuttle bus.

title: Walk the ramparts of Cartagena's walled Old City at sunset
description: Spanish engineers spent over two centuries building these walls to keep pirates out, thick enough in places to walk along the top the entire perimeter. Do the walk right before sunset - the heat drops, the light turns the pastel facades gold, and street vendors start selling cold lemonade from carts along the way.

title: Explore the tunnel network inside Castillo San Felipe de Barajas
description: Built to withstand British and French sieges, the fortress has a maze of interior tunnels designed so sound carries to alert defenders of an approaching enemy while confusing anyone who got inside. Bring a torch or your phone light; several of the original tunnels are unlit and genuinely dark.

title: Snorkel the coral reefs of the Rosario Islands by boat from Cartagena
description: This is a protected marine national park an hour by speedboat from Cartagena's harbour, though sediment from mainland rivers means visibility varies more than the postcard photos suggest. Public day-tour boats stop at more crowded islands; a private or small-group charter gets to quieter reefs further out.

title: Spend the day on the white sand of Playa Blanca, Baru
description: The sand here is genuinely white rather than the brownish Caribbean-adjacent tone of Cartagena's city beaches, reached by boat or a long causeway drive. Vendors work the beach constantly, offering everything from oysters to massages; a firm 'no gracias' is standard local etiquette, not rudeness.

title: Trek four days through jungle to reach Ciudad Perdida
description: Built by the Tairona people centuries before Machu Picchu and rediscovered by looters in 1972, the site is reached only on foot, over 1,200 stone steps up a final ridge. Guides are legally mandatory and only a handful of licensed agencies run the route, so book directly rather than through a generic online reseller.

title: Hike between jungle-backed beaches in Tayrona National Park
description: The park closes several weeks a year, usually in February and June, to let the ecosystem and Indigenous sacred sites rest from visitor numbers. Cabo San Juan's twin beaches either side of a rocky outcrop are the reward for the hour-plus walk in from the entrance; the closer beaches near the gate get crowded fast.

title: Cool off at a waterfall swimming hole above Minca
description: A 45-minute drive up from the Caribbean heat of Santa Marta into the Sierra Nevada foothills, Minca sits at a cooler altitude with coffee and cacao farms open for tours alongside several swimmable waterfalls. It's become the backpacker alternative base to Santa Marta for exploring the same mountain range.

title: Float down the Palomino River on an inner tube to the Caribbean
description: The river runs cold off the Sierra Nevada snowline and drifts you for around two hours down to where it meets the sea, so you can genuinely float from mountain water into salt water in one trip. Horseback riding along the same beach at sunset has become the other reason people stop here.

title: Watch the sunset from Santa Marta's malecon waterfront
description: Founded in 1525, it's the oldest surviving city in Colombia, though most travellers now use it purely as a jumping-off point for Tayrona and Ciudad Perdida rather than a destination itself. The waterfront promenade fills with local families and street food carts every evening once the coastal heat breaks.

title: See the five-colour river bloom at Cano Cristales
description: An endemic river plant turns sections of the riverbed red, yellow, green, blue and black for a few months each year, when water levels sit at exactly the right depth to let sunlight through without the current damaging the plant. The area was closed to tourism until 2009 due to armed conflict in the region, so infrastructure is still limited; access is via a short flight to La Macarena followed by a guided walk.

title: Walk beneath the towering wax palms of Cocora Valley
description: The Quindio wax palm is the world's tallest palm species, reaching up to 60m, and Colombia's national tree, growing only in this narrow band of Andean cloud forest. The full loop climbs into hummingbird-filled cloud forest before dropping back to the palm-studded valley floor; horses are available for anyone who'd rather not do the climb.

title: Wander the balconied streets of colourful Salento
description: The town's balconies and shopfronts are painted in the same bold colour blocks found across the coffee region, a tradition tied to the wealth 20th-century coffee exports brought to towns like it. Climb the Alto de la Cruz viewpoint steps at the end of Calle Real for a free look over the valley.

title: Pick and roast your own coffee at a Quindio finca
description: Small family fincas around Salento walk visitors through the entire process, from picking ripe red cherries to hand-roasting and grinding, rather than the industrial-scale tours found further into the coffee triangle. Harvest runs roughly October to December and April to June; visit outside those windows and there's less to actually pick.

title: Ride the outdoor escalators through Comuna 13's street art
description: Outdoor escalators were installed in 2011 to connect a hillside neighbourhood once considered Medellin's most dangerous, and local guides, many who grew up through the violence, now lead tours explaining the murals painted over that history. Hip-hop and breakdance performances happen informally most afternoons partway up the escalators.

title: Climb 700 steps up the Piedra del Penol for the view over Guatape
description: The 220m granite monolith was climbed for the first time only in 1954, using wooden pegs hammered into a crack in the rock, before the current staircase existed. From the top, the reservoir below splays out into countless finger-like inlets around flooded former farmland.

title: Photograph the painted zocalo panels of Guatape's streets
description: Nearly every building carries a colourful relief panel, a zocalo, depicting the trade or family history of whoever lives inside, a decorative tradition unique to this town. Rent a tuk-tuk (chiva) for a loop around the lakeshore if the Piedra steps have already worn out your legs.

Built as genuine public transit rather than a tourist gondola, the cable car system was Medellin's answer to connecting hillside barrios that buses and cars couldn't reach, and it costs the same single fare as any bus ride in the city. The line up to Parque Arvi ends in cloud forest and organic markets that most visitors who only do Comuna 13 and Guatape never see.
title: Ride the Metrocable over Medellin's hillside barrios to Parque Arvi
See a miniature Antioquian village replica at Pueblito Paisa
description: Built in 1978 on a hilltop park to preserve the look of a traditional Antioquian village as Medellin modernised around it, the replica includes a scaled-down church, plaza and typical houses. It's a short walk from Parque Poblado and better for the skyline view over the city than the recreation itself.

title: Cross the colonial bridge into Santa Fe de Antioquia
description: This colonial town predates Medellin as the region's original capital, and its 1895 suspension bridge, once the longest in South America, still carries foot traffic across the Cauca River. The heat here is a noticeable step up from Medellin's spring-like climate, despite being only a two-hour drive away.

title: Wander the colonial streets of Bogota's La Candelaria
description: Bogota sits at 2,640m, high enough that the altitude hits visitors before the colonial architecture does, so plan a slow first day. Graffiti tours through La Candelaria explain how Bogota became one of the world's most tolerated street-art cities, with much of it created legally rather than removed.

title: See pre-Columbian gold work at Bogota's Museo del Oro
description: The museum holds over 34,000 gold pieces from cultures that predate the Spanish by over a thousand years, including the small raft figure believed to have inspired the El Dorado legend. The dark, vault-like final room where the main collection is displayed is deliberately theatrical, meant to recreate a moment of ceremonial discovery.

title: Ride the cable car up Monserrate for sunset over Bogota
description: A 17th-century church sits at the 3,150m summit, still an active pilgrimage site, with a funicular and cable car both running up the same steep hillside above the city. Weekday afternoons are noticeably quieter than weekends, when Bogota residents themselves fill the walking trail up as a fitness hike.

title: Descend into the underground Salt Cathedral of Zipaquira
description: Carved directly into a working salt mine over 180m underground, the cathedral replaced an earlier, structurally unsound version built in the 1950s that had to be closed. Crosses and chapel details are cut straight from the salt walls themselves rather than added afterward, lit to look almost like ice.

title: Stargaze from the red-rock canyons of the Tatacoa Desert
description: Despite the name, this is a dry tropical forest rather than a true desert, eroded into red and grey badlands that split into two distinct coloured zones an hour's walk apart. An observatory near Villavieja runs telescope sessions most clear nights, taking advantage of skies with almost no competing light pollution.

title: Walk among ancient stone statues at San Agustin Archaeological Park
description: This is the largest collection of pre-Columbian religious monuments in South America, several hundred carved stone statues left by a culture that vanished before the Spanish arrived, with no written record explaining who made them or why. The park is remote enough that it gets a fraction of the visitors Colombia's coastal sites do, despite the UNESCO listing.

title: Snorkel the seven-colour sea off San Andres Island
description: Locals call the water around the island the 'sea of seven colours' for the visible gradient from shallow turquoise to deep navy blue over the surrounding reef shelf. It's geographically closer to Nicaragua than mainland Colombia, a leftover of a still-disputed maritime border, which is why flights connect through Bogota rather than any nearer capital.

title: Take a salsa lesson in Cali, the self-declared salsa capital of the world
description: Cali dancers add extra fast footwork and turns not found in Cuban or New York styles, developed in the city's salsa clubs since the genre arrived via Caribbean radio in the 1960s. Delirio, a nightly salsa circus show, is the polished version; a class at a local academy is the honest way to actually learn a few steps.

title: Cross Villa de Leyva's oversized cobblestone plaza
description: The main plaza is one of the largest cobbled squares in South America, deliberately oversized and left unshaded so colonial cavalry could muster and drill in it. The surrounding high desert is dotted with fossil sites; a local museum displays a nearly complete Kronosaurus skeleton found in the area.

title: See wild giant tortoises roam the highlands of Santa Cruz
description: Some individuals here live well past 100 years and can weigh over 250kg, and the highland reserves let you see them roaming freely rather than in the tortoise breeding centre's enclosures. Rainy season, roughly January to May, is when they're most active and visible in the open grass rather than buried in mud wallows.

title: Snorkel with sea lions and reef sharks at Los Tuneles, Isabela
description: Lava flows cooled into arches and tunnels just offshore, creating a natural aquarium where sea horses, reef sharks and sea turtles are regularly seen in the same hour. Access is by boat only, and the channel can only be crossed at certain tide levels, so trips run on the tide's schedule, not a fixed departure time.

title: Watch blue-footed boobies perform their mating dance on North Seymour
description: Males lift their bright blue feet in an exaggerated strut to attract females, a display so visually odd it's become the unofficial mascot behaviour of the whole archipelago. Frigatebirds nesting nearby inflate a red throat pouch the size of a balloon during the same courting season.

title: Watch marine iguanas bask by the thousand on Fernandina
description: This is the most volcanically active and least disturbed island in the archipelago, with no introduced species ever recorded, so the marine iguana colonies here are as close to an unaltered Galapagos as exists. They pile on top of each other in stacks to conserve heat after diving into cold water to feed on algae.

title: Learn how the Galapagos tortoise was pulled back from near-extinction
description: The breeding centre here raised Diego, a tortoise credited with fathering an estimated 800 offspring and single-handedly rebuilding his subspecies' population before retiring back to the wild in 2020. It's the most accessible way to see juvenile tortoises up close, since wild adults in the highlands keep more distance.

title: Walk the colonial plazas of Quito's UNESCO-listed Old Town
description: It was the first UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed anywhere, in 1978, recognised for having South America's best-preserved, largest historic centre. La Compania church alone reportedly used seven tonnes of gold leaf on its interior, best seen in late afternoon light through the west-facing doors.

title: Ride the TelefériQo cable car up Pichincha's slopes for the Quito skyline
description: The cable car climbs to nearly 4,000m on the flank of the active Pichincha volcano, well above Quito's own already-high 2,850m elevation, so altitude hits fast at the top. Marked trails continue further up toward the Rucu Pichincha summit for anyone acclimatised and equipped to keep going.

title: Stand with one foot in each hemisphere at Mitad del Mundo
description: The monument's painted line is a few hundred metres off the true equator, which GPS only pinpointed after the monument was already built; a separate museum nearby marks the accurate coordinate with balancing-an-egg and water-vortex demonstrations. Either spot makes the same photo, so most visitors don't bother chasing the more precise line.

title: Spot hummingbirds and the cock-of-the-rock in Mindo's cloud forest
description: Over 500 bird species have been recorded in this small cloud forest region, including leks where male Andean cock-of-the-rock gather at dawn to perform competitive displays for females. Zip-lines and tubing runs through the same forest give it a second life as an adrenaline day trip once the birdwatching wraps up.

title: Hike to the refuge on Cotopaxi, one of the world's highest active volcanoes
description: At 5,897m it's one of the highest active volcanoes on earth, and the hike to the Jose Rivas refuge at 4,864m is demanding enough on its own without attempting the glacier summit push beyond it. The national park around it also holds wild horses and Andean condors, visible even without going near the peak itself.

title: Hike the rim of the turquoise crater lake at Quilotoa
description: The lake fills a caldera left by an eruption roughly 800 years ago, and its colour shifts between green and turquoise depending on mineral concentration and light. The full rim circuit takes most of a day; the shorter option is the steep descent-and-climb-back down to the water's edge alone.

title: Soak in volcanic hot springs at Banos below Tungurahua volcano
description: The springs are fed by the still-active Tungurahua volcano looming directly over town, which last had a major eruption in 2006 and forced a full evacuation. The main public pool, La Piscina de la Virgen, is hottest right after dark and busiest with the same crowd doing the town's canyoning and rafting circuit by day.

title: Ride the Swing at the End of the World over the Tungurahua valley
description: The swing hangs from a rickety wooden treehouse at the edge of a cliff, built originally as a volcano observation post rather than a tourist ride, with Tungurahua smoking in full view when conditions allow. There's no harness; the height and lack of restraint are entirely the point.

title: Feel the spray from the Pailon del Diablo waterfall up close
description: The trail winds behind and directly beside the falls through carved rock tunnels, close enough that the mist alone will soak you before you reach the main viewing platform. It's one stop on Banos' 'Route of the Waterfalls', a cable-car-and-path circuit that strings together several falls along the same river gorge.

title: Bargain for handwoven textiles at the Otavalo Market
description: The Saturday market is one of the largest and oldest indigenous markets in the Americas, run by Otavaleno artisans who've exported textiles internationally since well before Ecuador itself existed as a country. Go early; by early afternoon the best stalls have sold out of their most distinctive weaving patterns.

title: Walk the riverside streets of colonial Cuenca
description: Four rivers run through this UNESCO-listed city, and its blue-domed New Cathedral was built with a footprint too large for its own foundations, forcing the towers to be left shorter than originally planned. It's also the real home of the Panama hat, hand-woven here long before the name got attached to Panama during canal construction.

title: Hike between glacial lakes in the paramo of Cajas National Park
description: Over 270 lakes are scattered across this high-altitude paramo ecosystem starting at 3,150m, connected by trails through twisted, moss-covered Polylepis forest found almost nowhere else on earth. Weather changes fast at this altitude; a clear morning can turn to fog and cold rain within the hour.

title: Ride the switchback tracks of the Devil's Nose train
description: Built in the early 1900s, the line climbs an almost sheer rock face by zigzagging back and forth on switchbacks rather than looping, a solution engineers reached after more conventional routes proved impossible. It was once nicknamed the most difficult railway in the world, and the workforce that built it suffered heavy losses to disease and the terrain.

title: Stand on Chimborazo, the point on Earth closest to space
description: Because Earth bulges at the equator, Chimborazo's summit is farther from the planet's core than Everest's, making it, by that measure, the closest point on the surface to outer space. Most visitors stop at the first refuge at around 4,800m; only trained climbers with permits continue toward the summit itself.

title: Spend the night in an Amazon lodge in Ecuador's Napo province
description: Ecuador's slice of Amazon rainforest around Tena and Coca gives access to the same biodiversity as Peru or Brazil's Amazon but with far shorter travel times from the capital, often under a day door to door. Community-run lodges, several owned and operated by Kichwa communities rather than outside operators, are common here and put more tourism income directly into local hands.

title: Soak in thermal pools with an Andean glacier view at Papallacta
description: The pools sit at nearly 3,300m on the road between Quito and the Amazon, fed by the same volcanic activity as Antisana, whose snow-capped peak is visible from the water on a clear day. It's a popular stop for travellers breaking up the drive down into the jungle rather than a standalone destination most people fly in for.

title: Bike down the Yungas 'Death Road' from La Paz
description: The old Yungas road drops 3,500m from La Cumbre pass at 4,650m to the jungle town of Coroico along a narrow gravel ledge with sheer drops, once blamed for hundreds of deaths a year before a paved bypass opened in 2006. Guided mountain-bike descents follow the old road for the thrill with a fraction of the old traffic risk.

title: Ride Mi Teleferico's cable cars across La Paz and El Alto
description: With ten lines strung across a canyon-bound city, this is the largest urban cable car network in the world, linking La Paz at the bottom of its bowl to El Alto perched 400m above on the rim. Ride it near sunset for a view over both cities lighting up at once.

title: Browse dried llama fetuses at La Paz's Witches' Market
description: Aymara traders sell dried llama foetuses to bury under new house foundations as an offering to Pachamama for good luck, alongside herbal remedies and amulets stacked along a steep cobbled street. Bargaining is expected, but the ritual items are not souvenirs - ask before you photograph a stall.

title: Walk the eroded spires of Valle de la Luna
description: Wind and rain have carved this clay-and-sandstone badland on the city's southern edge into a maze of spires and canyons, walkable on a marked loop trail in under an hour. It's a city bus ride from central La Paz, an easy half-afternoon add-on rather than a dedicated day trip.

title: Hike between Inca sites on Isla del Sol, Lake Titicaca
description: Inca mythology names this island the birthplace of the sun, and its ridge trail, walked north to south in around three hours, passes terraced fields and a sacred rock with no roads or cars anywhere on the island. The Bolivian side is reached by boat from Copacabana and sees far fewer visitors than Peru's stretch of the same lake.

title: Study the carved Gate of the Sun at Tiwanaku
description: This city was already an ancient ruin by the time the Inca arrived, its Gate of the Sun cut from a single block of andesite and covered in a carved calendar still not fully decoded. Archaeologists estimate less than ten percent of the site has been excavated, most of it still buried under the surrounding fields.

This was once the highest developed ski resort on Earth at 5,400m, until its glacier, one of the fastest-disappearing in the Andes, melted away completely by 2009, decades ahead of scientists' own projections. What's left is a bare rock summit and an abandoned ski hut, with a thin-air view over La Paz and the Cordillera Real.
title: Stand on Chacaltaya's summit where the glacier used to be
Drive across the mirror-flat expanse of the Uyuni salt flat
description: At over 10,000 square kilometres this is the largest salt flat on Earth, a dried prehistoric lakebed with a crust several metres thick. A thin film of rainwater between December and April turns the whole surface into a seamless mirror of the sky, while the dry months bring the cracked white hexagons and forced-perspective photos it's better known for.

title: Climb the giant cacti of Incahuasi Island mid-salt-flat
description: A coral-fossil outcrop rises straight out of the salt crust, covered in Trichocereus cacti, some over 900 years old and 12m tall, an odd green island on an otherwise all-white horizon. It's the standard lunch stop on salt flat tours, with a short summit trail giving a 360-degree view of the salar.

title: Climb over rusted engines at the Uyuni train cemetery
description: These British-built steam locomotives were abandoned in the open desert when Bolivia's mining export network collapsed in the 1940s, and decades of salt wind have rusted them into climbable sculpture. It's a free stop 3km outside Uyuni town, usually the first or last thing on a salt flat tour itinerary.

title: Descend into the still-active silver mines of Cerro Rico
description: This mountain funded the Spanish empire for two centuries and is estimated to have cost millions of forced and indentured labourers their lives; miners still work its narrow, unventilated tunnels by hand with dynamite today. Visitors buy gifts, coca leaves or soft drinks at the miners' market before entering, the expected way to thank the crews for the access.

title: Chase flamingos across the red water of Laguna Colorada
description: Algae and mineral sediment stain this high-altitude lake blood-red, and thousands of James's, Andean and Chilean flamingos wade through water so mineral-laden it barely freezes despite regular sub-zero nights. It's one stop on the standard three-day 4x4 circuit out of Uyuni, usually paired with the Sol de Manana geysers and the green-tinted Laguna Verde further south.

Hundreds of Cretaceous-era footprints press into an exposed rock shelf a short walk from the village, alongside a canyon trail and the Umajalanta cave system, deep enough to need ropes, headlamps and a local guide. Bolivia's least-visited national park despite being only a rough six-hour drive from Cochabamba.
title: Walk dinosaur tracks and cave systems in Torotoro National Park
Wander the whitewashed colonial centre of Sucre
description: A preservation ordinance requires every building in Bolivia's constitutional capital to stay whitewashed, so the skyline reads as unbroken white against red-tile roofs. The Casa de la Libertad on the main plaza holds the room where Bolivia's declaration of independence was signed in 1825.

title: See thousands of dinosaur footprints on the wall at Cal Orck'o
description: A cement quarry outside Sucre exposed a limestone wall that tectonic movement has since tilted to near-vertical, holding over 5,000 footprints from at least eight dinosaur species. Telescopes at the visitor platform are the only way to make out the tracks highest up the wall.

title: Tour the restored Jesuit mission churches of Chiquitania
