description: Six Jesuit mission towns built between 1696 and 1760 survived largely because the remoteness that isolated them also spared them from the demolition that hit similar missions elsewhere. A Swiss architect led a decades-long restoration starting in the 1970s; San Javier and Concepcion are the easiest pair to combine on a short circuit.

title: Puzzle over the carved rock temple of El Fuerte de Samaipata
description: A single sandstone outcrop is carved with channels, seats, niches and geometric shapes by the Chane, Inca and other cultures in turn, and archaeologists still disagree on whether its main purpose was ceremonial or astronomical. The hillside village of Samaipata makes an easy overnight base two hours from Santa Cruz.

title: Ride the cable car up to Cristo de la Concordia above Cochabamba
description: Measured a certain way, this statue edges out Rio's Christ the Redeemer by a few metres, a point of local pride Cochabambinos will happily explain to you. A cable car replaced the old staircase climb in 2019 and runs most days, except when high wind up on the ridge shuts it down.

title: Spend the night in a jungle lodge inside Madidi National Park
description: Rated among the most biodiverse protected areas on the planet, Madidi runs from Andean cloud forest down to Amazon lowland within a single park, reached by motorised canoe upriver from Rurrenabaque. Rurrenabaque itself is reachable only by small-plane flight or a rough multi-day bus ride from La Paz.

title: Spot caimans and pink river dolphins on a Beni pampas tour
description: The open wetland pampas around Rurrenabaque show far more wildlife in far less time than Madidi's dense jungle, caimans lining the riverbanks by the dozen and pink river dolphins that boatmen coax close with fish. Dry season concentrates animals around shrinking waterholes, the best sighting odds of the year.

title: Watch devil dancers lead Oruro's Carnaval parade
description: This UNESCO-recognised festival centres on La Diablada, the devil dance performed by miners' guilds as thanks to the Virgin of Socavon for protection underground. The main parade runs for upwards of twenty hours straight, so most visitors plan around a window rather than trying to catch all of it.

title: Eat parrilla at Montevideo's Mercado del Puerto
description: A 19th-century iron market hall in the old port is packed wall-to-wall with parrillas grilling short ribs and morcilla dulce, a sweet blood sausage, over open flame. Go for a late lunch on Saturday, when it's loudest and at its best.

title: Walk the Rambla along Montevideo's riverfront at sunset
description: At 22km this is one of the longest continuous waterfront promenades in the world, and locals fill it every evening carrying a thermos and mate gourd rather than a coffee cup. The Rio de la Plata is so wide here you can't see Argentina on the far side.

title: Stand pitch-side at Estadio Centenario, home of the first World Cup
description: Built in under nine months for the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, which Uruguay hosted and won, the attached football museum holds trophies and memorabilia from that tournament few visiting fans expect to find in Montevideo. It's still a working stadium, so match schedules can close parts of the museum on game days.

title: Watch sunset from the lighthouse over Colonia's cobblestones
description: Founded by the Portuguese in 1680 to smuggle goods past Spanish Buenos Aires across the river, the town swapped hands seven times and its mismatched Portuguese and Spanish street grids still collide at odd angles. Climb the 19th-century lighthouse, built inside the ruins of a convent, for the best view over the Rio de la Plata.

title: Pose with the fingers of La Mano rising from Punta del Este's sand
description: Chilean sculptor Mario Irarrazabal built these five giant concrete fingers in 1982 for an outdoor art event and never took them down, and they've since half-sunk into the dune that keeps shifting around them. Punta del Este itself swells from a sleepy town to South America's answer to the Hamptons every summer.

title: Watch the sunset bell ring at Casapueblo above Punta Ballena
description: Artist Carlos Paez Vilaro built this whitewashed, doorless, corner-free house-turned-hotel and gallery over 36 years, inspired by Mediterranean villages and Gaudi. Staff still ring a bell and play a recording of the artist's own words every evening at sunset, a ritual unchanged since his death in 2014.

title: Boat out to the sea lion colony on Isla de Lobos
description: The island holds one of the largest South American sea lion and fur seal colonies in the hemisphere, tens of thousands strong, and boats aren't permitted to land, only circle close. Uruguay's oldest lighthouse, lit since 1857, still operates on the island.

title: Reach car-free Cabo Polonio by truck over the dunes
description: No roads, grid electricity or phone signal reach the village; the only way in is a truck convoy over the dunes from the highway or a long walk along the beach. A sea lion colony hauls out on the rocks below the lighthouse, and September to November brings southern right whales close enough to watch from the point.

title: Surf and eat fresh-caught fish in Punta del Diablo
description: A working fishing village turned laid-back surf town, still small enough that boats haul the day's catch straight onto the sand outside the restaurants that will cook it that night. It gets far fewer Argentine and Brazilian crowds than Punta del Este, an hour's drive south.

title: Explore the star-shaped ramparts of Fortaleza de Santa Teresa
description: Built by the Portuguese in 1762 and captured by Spain before it was even finished, the fort anchors a national park with its own botanical garden and a stretch of empty Atlantic beach that most Punta del Este visitors never drive far enough north to see.

title: Taste tannat, Uruguay's signature red, at a Canelones bodega
description: Tannat arrived with Basque immigrants in the 1870s and turned softer and more approachable in Uruguay's climate than in its native southwest France, now the grape the country has built its wine identity around. Most bodegas here are a 40-minute drive from Montevideo and take same-day bookings outside harvest season.

title: Soak in the thermal pools of Termas del Dayman
description: Geothermal water rises at a near-constant 38-46C from wells drilled in the 1940s while prospecting for oil, feeding a complex of public and resort pools outside Salto. It's a popular winter escape for Uruguayans and Argentines alike, when the outdoor pools steam against the cold air.

title: Walk the riverside Costanera and Palacio de Lopez in Asuncion
description: The pink presidential palace overlooks the Paraguay River and is still an active seat of government, so entry is exterior-only. The Costanera promenade below was reclaimed from the river only in the last two decades, built over what used to be a flood-prone informal settlement.

title: Wander the ruins of Trinidad and Jesus, Paraguay's Jesuit missions
place: Jesuit Missions of Trinidad and Jesus
description: La Santisima Trinidad del Parana, the larger and better-preserved of the two UNESCO-listed missions, still has stone carvings of angels playing instruments used to teach Guarani converts European music; Jesus de Tavarangue, a short drive away, was left unfinished when the Jesuits were expelled in 1767. A single ticket covers both, an easy pairing in one day.

title: See the reconstructed Jesuit observatory at San Cosme y Damian
description: Jesuit priests here tracked eclipses and stars well enough to correspond with European astronomers of the day; a rebuilt observation tower and sundial garden now demonstrate the calculations they made without telescopes. It's the least-visited of Paraguay's three Jesuit mission sites, usually just a handful of visitors a day.

title: Watch the Monday River drop over Salto del Monday, near Ciudad del Este
description: At 40m this is actually taller than Niagara Falls, tucked a short drive from Ciudad del Este's border-town chaos and completely overshadowed by Iguazu 30km away. A catwalk leads out over the gorge close enough to feel the spray, with a fraction of its famous neighbour's crowds.

title: Visit the Mennonite colonies and dry Chaco wilderness around Filadelfia
description: German-speaking Mennonite farmers drained and settled this thorn-scrub wilderness starting in the 1930s, building dairy co-operatives that now anchor the regional economy. The surrounding Gran Chaco holds jaguars and tapirs, but roads are unpaved and distances huge, so this is a multi-day trip, not a day trip from Asuncion.

title: Stand where Paraguay's last stand of the Triple Alliance War ended
description: Marshal Francisco Solano Lopez was killed here in 1870, the final battle of a war that killed a majority of Paraguay's adult male population, a national wound the park treats as a memorial as much as a nature reserve. Weathered sandstone hills and a small waterfall inside see very few visitors given the historical weight of the site.

title: Swim below the waterfall in Ybycui National Park's old iron works
description: Paraguay's first iron foundry, built in the 1850s to arm the country before the Triple Alliance War, was bombed by Brazilian forces and now sits half-swallowed by rainforest beside the park's waterfall and swimming hole. It's one of the few national parks near Asuncion reachable in a single day trip.

title: Fly over the jungle to reach Angel Falls, the world's tallest waterfall
description: At 979m it drops nearly 15 times the height of Niagara off the edge of Auyantepui, and in the driest months the river approach can be too shallow for the motorised dugout canoes that ferry visitors upriver from Canaima. Flights in and out of Canaima are the only realistic way to reach the base camp - there's no road.

title: Trek five days up the flat summit of Mount Roraima
description: The sheer-sided tepui that inspired Arthur Conan Doyle's The Lost World rises 400m straight up from the Gran Sabana, and the only way to its summit plateau is a single ramp-like crack in the cliff face on the Venezuelan side. Endemic black frogs and carnivorous plants live nowhere else on Earth, isolated on top for millions of years.

title: Walk behind the curtain of Salto Sapo on Canaima Lagoon
description: A trail runs directly behind this waterfall's full curtain on the edge of Canaima Lagoon, close enough that the force of it soaks anyone who doesn't bag their camera first. It's a short boat ride from Canaima village, usually paired with the flight or river trip out to Angel Falls.

title: Island-hop the coral cays of Los Roques by boat
description: A protected archipelago of over 300 cays and reefs with water clarity regularly compared to the Maldives, reachable only by small aircraft from Caracas since there's no way in by road or ferry. Cayo de Agua and Crasqui are the two most-requested day-trip islands from the main settlement, Gran Roque.

title: Ride the Merida cable car high into the Venezuelan Andes
description: When running at full length this is one of the highest and longest cable car systems in the world, climbing from the city to over 4,700m near Pico Espejo in four stages. Service has been repeatedly suspended for maintenance over the years, so it's worth confirming which stages are actually running before planning around it.

title: Sandboard the wind-carved dunes of Medanos de Coro
description: These shifting dunes sit improbably between a colonial desert town and the Caribbean, built from sand blown in off the coast rather than any local rock. Cross in the early morning or late afternoon - the white sand at midday gets hot enough to burn bare feet.

title: Reach the Caribbean beaches of Choroni over the cloud-forest pass
description: The road in from Maracay switchbacks through Henri Pittier National Park's cloud forest, one of the oldest national parks in the Americas, before dropping to a Spanish colonial village and a run of dark-sand bays. Puerto Colombia's fishing boats still sell the morning's catch straight off the beach.

title: Climb the wooden spire of St. George's Cathedral in Georgetown
description: Built in 1892 and still among the tallest wooden buildings on Earth at over 43m, its entire frame including the spire was built from local greenheart and other tropical hardwoods without structural steel. Pair it with Stabroek Market's cast-iron clock tower a few blocks away, shipped from England in prefabricated pieces in the 1880s.

title: Fly over the jungle to Kaieteur, the world's largest single-drop falls by volume
description: At 226m Kaieteur is roughly five times the height of Niagara, and unlike most falls this dramatic it has almost no barriers, viewing platforms sit right at the unfenced cliff edge above the drop. Most visitors fly in on a small charter for a few hours; there's no road, and the multi-day hike in is for the committed only.

title: Cross the treetop canopy walkway in Iwokrama Forest
description: Suspended up to 30m above the forest floor across four linked platforms, the walkway puts you at eye level with a rainforest canopy that holds one of the highest concentrations of bat species recorded anywhere. Night walks from the nearby field station give the best odds of the reserve's elusive jaguars and tapirs, though most visitors leave having heard rather than seen one.

title: Watch giant river otters fish at Karanambu Ranch
description: The ranch's rehabilitated giant otters, some raised from orphaned pups, still return each day to fish the oxbow lake in front of the lodge, alongside wild families that were never captive. It's also one of the more reliable places in South America to spot the arapaima, a fish that can grow past two metres and has to surface every few minutes to breathe.

title: Ride out across the Rupununi savanna from a cattle ranch
description: Cattle ranches dating back over a century run alongside Wapishana and Macushi villages across this flat, seasonally flooded grassland the size of a small country, reached by a single dirt road or a light aircraft from Georgetown. Roads through the savanna disappear under the rains between roughly May and August, so travel timing is dictated by water, not preference.

title: Watch leatherback turtles nest after dark on Shell Beach
description: This stretch of the northwest coast, made of eroded shell fragments rather than sand, hosts one of the largest leatherback turtle nesting populations in the region, alongside green and hawksbill turtles. There's no hotel infrastructure; visitors stay in a small conservation camp run with the local Arawak community that patrols the beach against poaching.

title: Walk Paramaribo's wooden colonial waterfront at Waterkant
description: Dutch, French and English colonists all left their mark on this UNESCO-listed centre, where white wooden mansions with green shutters line streets a few blocks from Fort Zeelandia. A synagogue and a mosque stand directly beside each other on Keizerstraat, long cited locally as proof of the city's easy religious mix.

title: Climb the granite dome of Voltzberg deep in Central Suriname Nature Reserve
description: Almost a tenth of Suriname's entire land area is protected inside this reserve, one of the largest tracts of untouched tropical rainforest left on Earth, reachable only by light aircraft and dugout canoe up the Coppename River. The pre-dawn scramble up Voltzberg's bare granite dome rewards with a sunrise view over unbroken canopy in every direction, howler monkey calls included.

title: Watch howler monkeys from the Brownsberg overlook above the Brokopondo reservoir
description: The reservoir below was flooded in the 1960s to power a Suriname aluminium smelter, drowning forest whose dead tree trunks still poke through the surface decades later. Brownsberg's ridge-top trails are an easy day trip from Paramaribo and give a realistic shot at eight monkey species without the flight needed to reach the deep interior.

title: Watch sea turtles nest on the beaches of Galibi Nature Reserve
description: Leatherback, green and olive ridley turtles all nest on this Marowijne River-mouth coastline, managed jointly with the Kalina Amerindian villages who run the guiding and lodges. Reaching it means a road and river journey from Paramaribo of several hours, with no shortcut.

title: Find the ruined synagogue of Jodensavanne in the jungle
description: Portuguese-Jewish planters built the Americas' first Jewish settlement with religious autonomy here in the 1600s, complete with the hemisphere's oldest synagogue ruins, before yellow fever and slave rebellions emptied it out. The brick foundations and overgrown cemetery now sit quietly back inside the rainforest an hour south of Paramaribo.

title: Feel a rocket launch shake the ground at Kourou's space centre
description: Europe's spaceport sits this close to the equator because the extra rotational speed cuts the fuel needed to reach orbit, and public viewing sites let you feel the shockwave several kilometres out when Ariane or Vega rockets go up. Launch dates shift constantly with weather and technical holds, so treat any booked date as provisional until the week of.

title: Boat out to Devil's Island, France's most notorious penal colony
description: The Salvation Islands held political prisoners and hardened convicts from 1852 until the penal colony finally closed in 1953, and Devil's Island itself, reserved for the regime's most dangerous political prisoners, is the one island boats aren't allowed to land on. Strong currents between the islands were as effective a deterrent to escape as any wall.

title: Walk the cell blocks of Camp de la Transportation
description: Every convict sentenced to France's Guiana penal colony passed through this transit camp on the Maroni River before being assigned to a labour camp or the offshore islands, and its solitary confinement cells are preserved much as they were left. The riverside town itself, founded by the prison administration, still has that penal-colony-turned-outpost feel.

title: Wander the colonial streets around Cayenne's Place des Palmistes
description: Royal palms planted in the 19th century still line this main square, ringed by pastel Creole colonial buildings and a market that spills out with Hmong, Creole and Brazilian produce side by side. Cayenne is a genuinely mixed-heritage town, worth an amble rather than a checklist stop.

title: Spotlight black caimans from a canoe on the Kaw Marsh at night
description: This flooded savanna and mangrove marsh holds one of the highest densities of black caiman in the Guianas, some well over four metres, best found by torchlight when their eyes catch the beam red. Overnight stays in the marsh village of Yandia put you on the water at dusk and dawn, the two windows when the caimans and howler monkeys are most active.

title: Walk beneath the whalebone arch at Stanley's Christ Church Cathedral
description: The arch out front is built from the jawbones of two blue whales, raised in 1933 to mark a century of British administration, and the cathedral itself is the southernmost Anglican cathedral in the world. Stanley's waterfront still runs on red phone boxes and left-hand traffic, a determinedly British outpost 8,000 miles from London.

title: Walk among thousands of king penguins at Volunteer Point
description: The largest king penguin colony in the Falklands numbers in the thousands, and there's no fence or boardwalk - visitors sit on the sand at a respectful distance and let the birds set the terms. The drive out from Stanley crosses several hours of trackless camp (open farmland), the last stretch passable only by 4x4.

title: Watch Magellanic penguins waddle to their burrows at Gypsy Cove
description: A 20-minute drive from Stanley, this is the easiest wildlife encounter in the Falklands - Magellanic penguins nest in burrows right along the dune path, most active around dusk when they return from fishing. Sections of the beach are still fenced off for old minefields left from the 1982 war, clearly marked and no real obstacle to the walk.

title: Watch elephant seals wallow on the beaches of Sea Lion Island
description: The southernmost inhabited island in the Falklands packs in elephant seals, sea lions, five penguin species and enough orcas patrolling the shallows at high tide to make them a genuine, if unpredictable, sighting. There's a single small lodge on the island, and flights in are by light aircraft only.

title: Sit among nesting albatross and rockhopper penguins on West Point Island
description: Black-browed albatross and southern rockhopper penguins nest side by side in tussac grass on the island's cliffs, close enough to watch the albatross's clattering courtship dance without a lens. It's a private island reached by boat from Carcass Island or by charter flight, with a farmhouse tea on offer as part of the visit.

title: Kayak the river channels of the Tigre Delta
description: An hour north of the city by train, the Parana delta breaks into hundreds of channels lined with stilt houses reached only by water. Paddle rather than take a tour boat - the narrow side streams are where the boats cannot go.
